meta.title: This AI experiment should get every investor's attention
meta.thread_line: 3 threads · Mercor's accountants-vs-Claude study, AI's first visible dent in the labor data, and the intelligence trade one sector at a time (newsletter, not a video)

snapshot: Source is Pompliano's daily newsletter, not a video; the book-launch promo, sponsor reads and podcast plug are excluded.
Mercor study: 12 licensed accountants scored **~37%** on real accounting tasks in 30-180 minutes; Claude Opus 5 scored **100%** on 20 of 20 solo attempts, each in under 10 minutes.
The surprise: accountants **working with Claude** were ~15x slower than Claude alone — human-plus-AI lost to AI alone.
Pompliano's view: accountants won't disappear; the job changes, like Excel replacing floors of bookkeepers. Mercor, Ramp and others agree AI still can't close a company's books alone.
Labor data (Warren Pies): since mid-2025, finance and tech **-246k jobs**, all other industries **+812k** — expected to intensify and spread next year.
Steve Rattner (NYT op-ed): since 1830 technology cut the workweek from 69 to 38 hours and raised real income per person ~20x.
Will Manidis: if even 1/10th of the AI story is real, every equity is mispriced — but the market prices it one trade at a time: "memories, then semis, then ____."

themes.status: MERCOR STUDY · 12 ACCOUNTANTS VS FRONTIER MODELS
themes.title: Claude Opus 5 scored 100% where experienced accountants scored ~37%
themes.lead: A frontier model beat senior accountants on real tasks, and adding the human to the loop made the work slower, not better.
bullets: **Mercor** pitted 12 licensed accountants (avg 5.4 years' experience, 10 of 12 senior or managers, half Big Four alumni) against frontier models on real-world accounting tasks.
Humans scored ~**37%**, taking 30-180 minutes per task.
Claude Opus 5 scored 100% on all 20 solo attempts, finishing each in under 10 minutes.
Accountants allowed to use Claude were still slower and less accurate: those sessions ran about **15x** slower than Claude alone.
Limit: Mercor, **Ramp** and other evaluators agreed AI still can't close a company's books by itself.

quote.text: This doesn't mean accountants are replaceable. But it does suggest the job will change significantly, even if model progress stalled today.

themes.watch: Mercor sells AI evaluation and training work, so a strong model result fits its business; the study is small (12 people, 20 attempts).

names.name: Mercor
names.blurb: Ran and published the accountants-vs-frontier-models study.

names.name: Ramp
names.blurb: Among the companies that evaluated the results; agreed AI can't yet close books alone.

themes.title: AI's first visible dent: finance and tech down 246k jobs while everything else adds 812k
themes.lead: Pompliano expects tasks, not roles, to vanish, and calls the fear headlines noise, while conceding the job data already shows AI pressure in finance and tech.
bullets: Warren Pies: since mid-2025, finance and tech industries are **-246k jobs**, all other industries +812k; he expects it to intensify next year and spread to other industries.
Pompliano's analogy: big companies once had floors of people doing the books; **Excel** replaced most of those hours, yet finance teams still employ plenty of people.
Expect accountants to shift to higher-value work even if AI eventually closes books on its own.
Steve Rattner's New York Times op-ed: since 1830, technology cut the US workweek from **69 to 38 hours** and raised real income per person roughly 20-fold — "properly managed, A.I. can do the same."
His bottom line: no human should spend their time on menial tasks software can automate.

quote.text: You are going to see scary headlines and lots of fear-mongering, but all that is just noise in my opinion.

themes.watch: Pompliano concedes some job impact as companies find AI's limits and workers retrain; the -246k figure is Pies' read of the data, not his.

themes.title: Every equity is mispriced, but the market reprices one sector at a time
themes.lead: Manidis' framing: if even a fraction of the AI story is real, mispricing is universal, and the market can only process it sequentially — memory first, then semis, then something next.
bullets: Manidis: "if you even believe 1/10th of this is real" then every single equity is drastically mispriced one way or another.
The market processes it **one trade at a time**: memories, then semis, then a blank — the next sector to reprice is the open question.
Pompliano's close: "the acceleration is just beginning" — hold on long enough to enjoy the ride.
themes.watch: Pompliano runs ProCap Financial (Nasdaq: SVIA); an accelerating-AI market narrative suits his business.

takeaways.title: Benchmark your own team's routine tasks against a frontier model solo, not just human-plus-AI.
Track finance and tech payrolls against the rest of the economy for AI displacement spreading.
Ask which sector reprices after memory and semis, and position before it's consensus.
Shift accounting and finance roles toward judgment work models still can't do, like closing the books.

hot_takes.take: You are going to see scary headlines and lots of fear-mongering, but all that is just noise in my opinion.
This dynamic will most likely intensify next year and expand into other industries.
If you even believe 1/10th of this is real, than every single equity is drastically mispriced in one way or another.
No human should be required to spend their precious time on Earth doing menial tasks that can be automated by software.

claims.claim: AI-driven job losses in finance and tech intensify next year and spread to other industries.
The market reprices AI one sector at a time: memory, then semis, then another sector.
claims.condition: if even 1/10th of the AI story is real
